title: Know Your Site

learn.summary: Before buying a single plant, spend a week learning what your yard actually offers: hours of direct sun, your USDA hardiness zone, and your average first and last frost dates. Most vegetables and fruiting plants need 6-8 hours of direct sun; leafy greens get by on 3-4. Plants fail more often from wrong-place placement than from bad care.

do: Walk your yard at 9am, noon, and 4pm this week and sketch which areas get direct sun at each check-in
Look up your USDA zone and last spring frost date and write both at the front of a garden notebook

children.title: Sun Mapping

learn.summary: Full sun means 6+ hours of direct light, part sun 4-6, part shade 2-4, full shade under 2. Sun angles shift dramatically between June and September, so a spot that is full sun in midsummer can be part shade by fall. Map before you plant: tomatoes, peppers, and squash sulk below 6 hours.

do: Pick your three sunniest spots from your sun sketch and label each full sun, part sun, or part shade with hour counts

children.title: Hardiness Zones

learn.summary: USDA zones are 10°F bands of average annual minimum winter temperature, split into 5°F half-zones (7a, 7b). They tell you which perennials, trees, and shrubs survive your winter — nothing about summer heat, rainfall, or soil. Buy perennials rated at least to your zone, ideally one zone hardier.

do: Check the zone rating on three perennials you own or want, and flag any rated less hardy than your zone

children.title: Frost Dates

learn.summary: Your average last spring frost and first fall frost bracket the growing season; the days between are what a seed packet means by "days to maturity" runway. These are 50/50 averages, not guarantees — a light frost (28-32°F) kills basil and tomatoes but sweetens kale and carrots. Count backward from frost dates to schedule every sowing.

do: Calculate your season length in days (last spring frost to first fall frost) and compare it to the days-to-maturity on two seed packets

children.title: Microclimates

learn.summary: A south-facing brick wall, a low frost pocket, or a windy corner can differ from the rest of your yard by an effective half zone or more. Masonry stores daytime heat and releases it at night; cold air flows downhill and pools in dips. Use warm microclimates to push marginal plants like figs or rosemary in cold zones.

do: On a frosty or cold morning, note where frost lingers longest and melts first in your yard — mark both spots on your sun map
